AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/CSC 计算机科学/Topic 1 ·: Three basic flows of program execution. Sequence executes in written order; selection tests with IF...THEN...ELSE...END IF or CASE and then takes a branch; iteration comes in three kinds: the fixed-count FOR loop, the pre-test WHILE loop (condition tested first, so it may run zero times) and the post-test REPEAT...UNTIL loop (runs at least once). Exam point: CASE can only compare a single value and cannot test a range, so use IF for ranges; a common mistake is confusing how many times pre-test and post-test loops run.

Variables are classed by what they store into four types: integer, float, string and Boolean. The type decides which operations are available: integers for counting and numbering, floats for measurement and averages, strings wrapped in quotes and joined with +, Booleans taking only True/False and often used as loop flags. Common mistakes are type mismatches that break an operation or lose precision, and forgetting that in Python input() returns a string that must be converted before it can take part in arithmetic.

Operators fall into three groups by function: arithmetic, covering add, subtract, multiply, divide, integer division DIV (or //) and remainder MOD (or %); relational, covering ==, !=, >, <, >=, <=, which give a Boolean result; and logical, covering AND, OR, NOT. Precedence from high to low is brackets, arithmetic, relational, NOT, AND, OR, and equal precedence goes left to right. Common mistakes are mixing up assignment = with comparison ==, and forgetting that MOD gives the remainder while DIV gives only the integer quotient.

Break a large problem into separate subprograms, each completing one logical task, so the code is easy to reuse, develop in parallel and debug. Parameters go in the brackets at definition, arguments are passed in at the call, and RETURN sends a result back (a function can return only a single value or a single data structure). The exam points are the two criteria that each subprogram does one thing and that the main program only makes calls; common mistakes are passing arguments in the wrong order, or piling all the logic into the main program.

Scope is the range in which a variable can be accessed. A local variable is defined inside a function, is valid only there and is released when the function ends; a global variable is defined outside the main program and can be read by several functions, and the convention is to initialise it outside the mainline function. The principle is to avoid global variables as far as possible, because they cause unexpected changes that are hard to trace. Common mistake: a function that means to change a global but does not declare it really just creates a local of the same name, so the outside value never changes.

How data is handed to the parameters when a function is called. Passing by value passes a copy, so changes inside the function do not affect the caller's variable; passing by reference passes the address, so changes inside the function alter the original data directly. In Python, immutable objects (integers, strings, tuples) behave as pass by value, while mutable objects (lists, dictionaries) behave as pass by reference. Common mistake: assuming everything is passed by value, so a list changed inside the function unexpectedly alters the outside data.

Three containers for holding data in bulk. A one-dimensional array uses an index to reach ordered elements of the same type; a two-dimensional array is a nested list located by two indices for row and column; a dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks values up quickly by key, with keys, values and items to get all the keys, values or pairs. Exam point: indices start at 0. Common mistakes are index out of range causing a runtime error, and writing the row and column order the wrong way round on a 2D array.

SCSA's writing conventions: keywords in full capitals, indentation showing the level of each control structure, every structure explicitly closed (IF...END IF, END WHILE, END FOR), a single equals sign for assignment and a double equals for comparison, variables initialised at the start of a module, constants declared with CONST in capitals, and global variables initialised outside the main program. Marks are usually lost for a missing END, using = as a comparison, an uninitialised counter, and messy indentation.

The first stage of the technology process: the job is to understand the problem, not to rush into code. First describe the current situation and the pain points, then split the requirements into functional and non-functional, and finally use a Gantt chart to lay out tasks, owners and dates as a schedule. The resulting requirement list is the basis for design and for acceptance testing later. Common mistakes are skipping requirements and coding straight away, or treating the Gantt chart as decoration so acceptance cannot be judged against the requirements.

The last three stages of the technology process. Design: choose the data structures (array, dictionary, 2D array), draw up the algorithm and check it by hand with test data first; develop: write the code to the design, debug it and run unit tests; evaluate: have real users carry out acceptance testing and review as the developer where it could be improved. The whole process is iterative, so problems found in evaluation send you back to design or development. Common mistakes are getting the four stages out of order, or leaving out unit testing and user acceptance testing.

A linear approach (waterfall) moves through requirements, design, coding, testing and delivery in order, each step finished before the next begins, and suits projects whose requirements are clear and stable; an iterative approach (Agile, the iterative route of the SDLC) delivers in several small rounds, each containing design, development and feedback, and suits projects whose requirements will change or whose deadline is tight and which need early results. The answering point is to choose on requirement stability and time pressure and justify the choice. Common mistake: saying both are more efficient without giving criteria.

The first four good programming practices. Validate input: check type and range before using data, and prompt and re-read if it fails. Clear and concise mainline: the main program only drives the flow, with all detail in subprograms. One logical task per subprogram: each does a single job. Stubs: build the structure first with empty functions that return only placeholder values, so the whole thing runs and can be tested piece by piece. Common mistakes are calculating with unvalidated input, or stuffing detailed logic into the mainline.

The other eight practices. Easy maintenance: meaningful names, comments, clear structure. Version control: keep a history of changes you can roll back and compare. Regular backups: prevent unrecoverable data loss. Identify social and ethical issues: consider privacy, security and fairness. Exception handling: catch errors with try...except so the program does not crash. Functions return only a single value or a single data structure. Also choose control structures and data structures appropriately. Common mistake: writing only that code should be tidy without saying what that means in practice.

Big O describes how the number of operations grows with the data size n, not an actual running time. This course requires you to recognise: linear search O(n), binary search O(log n), bubble sort O(n²), insertion sort O(n²) but O(n) in the best case, and selection sort always O(n²); with a swap flag, bubble sort also reaches O(n) in the best case. Common mistakes are reading O(log n) as half the time, or confusing it with the best and worst cases.

Linear search compares items one by one from the start, returning the index as soon as it finds the target and -1 if it does not; the data need not be sorted and the worst case inspects all n items, so it is O(n). Binary search compares the middle value with the target and discards half according to the ordering, taking O(log n) comparisons, so a million sorted records need at most about 20. The exam point is to state that binary search requires sorted data, and that linear search is the better choice for unsorted or small data sets.

All three use nested loops and take O(n²) time. Bubble: repeatedly compare adjacent items and swap them, pushing the largest value to the end each pass. Insertion: take each element and insert it into the correct position in the already sorted part in front, like sorting a hand of cards, reaching O(n) in the best case when the data is nearly ordered. Selection: each pass finds the smallest value in the unsorted region and swaps it to the front, with a fixed n(n-1)/2 comparisons. The exam asks when insertion beats selection: when the data is already almost sorted.

Testing happens at several levels. Unit testing verifies one function or module at a time; integration and system testing check that modules work together; acceptance testing has users confirm that the functional requirements are met; live testing uses data close to the real environment and looks at file size, the mix of transaction types and response times; load testing checks how the system performs under large data volumes or high concurrency. Test data should include normal, boundary and invalid values. Common mistake: declaring testing finished after a few normal values of your own.

Three kinds of error you must tell apart. A syntax error breaks the rules of the language, so the program will not run at all and the message names the line. A logic error runs but gives wrong results, the compiler reports nothing and it is the hardest to locate, so you can only compare against expected output. A runtime error interrupts the program while it executes because of the environment or the data, typically divide by zero, index out of range or a connection timeout. The exam point is classifying a described symptom: it ran most of the way and then stopped is usually a runtime error.

Common ways to track a fault down. Breakpoints: pause the program on a suspect line, step through and watch each variable's current value. Print statements: output intermediate results at key points to narrow the error down. Hand checking and desk checking: take test data and work through each variable line by line, comparing results with expected output to find the first line that diverges. Common mistakes are changing code on a hunch instead of locating the fault first, or setting so many breakpoints that no pattern is visible.

Organising a program with classes as templates and objects as instances. Attributes hold data and methods define behaviour; encapsulation hides internal detail and exposes only the necessary interface; inheritance lets a subclass reuse and extend the features of its parent; polymorphism makes the same method call behave differently on different objects; abstraction keeps only the necessary features. Creating an object from a class is instantiation. The exam points are telling class from object and inheritance from instantiation. Common mistakes are using a class directly as an object, or missing what encapsulation and polymorphism mean.

The hands-on side: define a class with class, set attributes in __init__, use self to refer to the current object, then instantiate an object and call its methods; extend it with class Subclass(Parent), where the subclass can override parent methods; inside a method you can equally use variables, conditionals and loops. Common mistakes are leaving self out of a method's parameters, writing __int__ instead of __init__, or forgetting to call the parent initialiser when inheriting so attributes go missing.

A developer's rights and responsibilities: respect and credit other people's intellectual property, including code, images, data and algorithms, while protecting your own work; follow industry and workplace codes of conduct (such as an ICT code of conduct); never write or distribute malware; and further, ensure software quality, respond to user feedback promptly, protect user privacy, and take account of ergonomic and accessibility needs. Common mistakes are copying code from the internet as your own work, or ignoring privacy and accessibility requirements.

Software is deeply embedded in society, and the impacts include: malware causing data and financial loss; heavy social dependence on software, so that a system failure drags down transport, health care and payments; social networks changing how we communicate while bringing privacy problems and cyberbullying; cyber security bearing directly on personal and national safety; and the mass of information online being unsourced, unverifiable, misleading or simply wrong. Answer these questions concretely rather than listing phenomena.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/CSC 计算机科学/Topic 2 ·: OSI divides network communication into seven layers. From the bottom: the physical layer (transmits bits as electrical or light signals), the data link layer (forwards frames inside one LAN using MAC addresses and divides collision domains), the network layer (routes by IP address and chooses the best path), the transport layer (ensures data arrives as expected), the session layer (manages connections between endpoints), the presentation layer (data format conversion, encryption and decryption) and the application layer (user application protocols). The exam point is saying why switches work at layer 2 and routers at layer 3.

The simplified four-layer model the real internet uses. From the bottom: network (the network access layer, matching OSI's physical and data link layers), internet (the internet layer, IP addressing and routing), transport (TCP and UDP) and application (merging OSI's session, presentation and application layers). Its key features are independent layers, IP at the centre and end-to-end responsibility for reliability. Common mistakes are getting the order of the four layers wrong, or confusing the internet layer with the network layer.

The two models describe the same thing and differ in the granularity of their layers. OSI has seven layers, is the reference model used in teaching and by vendors, and splits application-related functions into session, presentation and application; DoD TCP/IP has only four layers, is the protocol stack actually in use, merges the physical and data link layers into network access and merges the top three into application. An answer must say which layer was merged or refined. Common mistake: reciting the layer names without being able to state the correspondence.

Protocols that serve user applications directly: SMTP sends email, FTP transfers files, HTTP and HTTPS read and write web pages (HTTPS being the encrypted version), DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses and other network parameters, DNS resolves domain names into IP addresses, and PING tests whether a host is reachable. The exam point is choosing a protocol for a scenario, for example HTTPS to visit a website or DNS to resolve a domain name. Common mistakes are mixing up FTP and HTTP, or treating PING as a transport protocol.

The transport layer handles end-to-end delivery of data. TCP is connection-oriented, reliable and ordered: a handshake establishes the connection and sequence and acknowledgement numbers keep data from being lost or reordered, at the cost of higher overhead. UDP is connectionless with low overhead and high speed but guarantees neither delivery nor order, which suits real-time use. TLS provides encryption above transport so that the contents of protocols such as HTTPS cannot be eavesdropped on or tampered with. The exam point is choosing TCP or UDP according to whether accuracy or speed matters.

The internet layer uses IPv4 (32-bit addresses, about 4.3 billion, now exhausted) and IPv6 (128-bit addresses, effectively unlimited, with a simpler header and native encryption support) to identify and address hosts, and ARP resolves an IP address into a MAC address so a frame can be delivered within the same subnet; the network access layer is defined by Ethernet (802.3, wired) and Wi-Fi (802.11, wireless), which set the frame format and the media access method. Common mistakes are placing ARP in the application layer, or saying Ethernet works at the network layer.

Three comparisons. Connection: TCP is connection-oriented and UDP is connectionless. Reliability: TCP uses sequence and acknowledgement numbers to keep data ordered and complete and retransmits lost packets, while UDP guarantees neither delivery nor order. Packet structure: the TCP header is at least 20 bytes (sequence number, acknowledgement number, window and other fields) whereas the UDP header is only 8 bytes, so the lower overhead makes UDP faster. An answer should choose for a specific application and justify it. Common mistake: knowing only that TCP is reliable and UDP is not, without the difference in cost.

Private addresses are used only inside a LAN and cannot be routed on the internet (10.x.x.x, 172.16-172.31.x.x, 192.168.x.x), and going online requires NAT to translate them into a public address. The subnet mask separates network bits from host bits, CIDR notation writes it as /prefix length, and the number of usable hosts is 2 to the power of (32 minus the prefix), minus 2. The default gateway is the exit address for leaving the local subnet, DNS resolves domain names into IP addresses, and port numbers identify specific services. Common mistake: forgetting to subtract 2 from the host count.

IPv4 addresses are classed by their first octet, and the course maps them onto three common **private** ranges: 10.0.0.0/8 (mask 255.0.0.0), 172.16.0.0/12 (mask 255.240.0.0) and 192.168.0.0/16 (mask 255.255.255.0). **The 172 range is the one people get wrong**: class B has a default mask of /16, i.e. 255.255.0.0, but the private range 172.16.0.0 uses /12, whose mask is 255.240.0.0 — the two are not the same thing. Usable hosts = 2^(32 - prefix) - 2; do not forget the minus 2.

Steps: first see how many subnets are needed and take the smallest k such that 2 to the power of k is at least the number of subnets, which means borrowing k bits from the host part so the new prefix is the old prefix plus k; the block size is 256 minus the non-255 value in the last octet of the mask; in each block the first address is the network address and the last is the broadcast address, and only the addresses between them can be assigned to hosts. Example: splitting a /24 into 2 subnets borrows 1 bit for /25 with block size 128. Common mistake: forgetting to deduct the network and broadcast addresses.

Data is encapsulated from the top down: the application layer produces data; the transport layer adds a TCP/UDP header to make a segment; the network layer adds an IP header to make a packet; the data link layer adds a frame header and trailer to make a frame; and the physical layer turns it into bits on the medium. The receiving end strips the headers layer by layer to recover the data. You must be able to say what each layer adds and who it hands to. Common mistakes are getting packet, frame and segment out of order, or dropping one of the layers.

The components work at different layers: transmission media (twisted pair, fibre, radio waves) carry signals at the physical layer; a modem converts between digital and analogue signals; a router uses IP addresses to choose paths at the network layer and joins different networks; a gateway translates between networks that use different protocols; a switch forwards frames by MAC address at the data link layer; a wireless access point connects wireless devices to the wired network; and a firewall filters traffic in and out by rules, usually sitting outside the trusted network. Common mistake: swapping the layers that routers and switches work at.

On architecture, client-server has a central server supplying resources, which is easy to manage centrally but brings a single point of failure and cost pressure, while in peer-to-peer all nodes are equal, which is cheap but hard to control. On scope, a LAN is small and a WAN spans regions. Common topologies are star (easy to manage, but a failure at the centre takes the whole network down), mesh (high redundancy, high cost) and hybrid. A VLAN divides subnets logically without changing the physical cabling; each switch port is its own collision domain, and broadcast domains must be divided by VLANs or routers.

Bandwidth is the maximum amount of data that can pass along a path per unit time, measured in bps rather than bytes per second, and too little of it causes congestion and delay. Design that balances performance and security: use higher-bandwidth links, use switches and VLANs to cut broadcast traffic, give priority to critical traffic, add redundant links and a suitable topology for fault tolerance, and monitor traffic continuously so anomalies are found in time. Common mistake: confusing bandwidth with actual throughput.

ping sends probe packets to a target to see whether it is reachable and reports the round-trip time and packet loss, which is used to judge connectivity and latency; traceroute (written tracert on Windows) shows every router a packet passes hop by hop with the time for each, which is used to locate which segment is slow or broken. The troubleshooting order is to ping the gateway and the target to confirm reachability, then traceroute to see which hop it sticks at. Common mistake: swapping what the two tools are for.

Draw with Cisco standard icons so the device types are distinguishable: routers, switches, modems, wireless access points and firewalls are intermediary devices handling forwarding and security; servers, desktops and the like are end devices, the start and end points of data; lines between devices show links and can be labelled with interfaces and subnet addresses. A proper diagram shows the hierarchy, the subnet divisions and the security boundary. Common mistakes are mixing icons, leaving out end devices, or forgetting to label subnets.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/CSC 计算机科学/Topic 3 ·: The Privacy Act 1988 is Australia's basic privacy law and governs how personal information is collected, stored, used and disclosed; APP 11 within it requires organisations to take reasonable steps to protect personal information from misuse, interference, loss, unauthorised access, modification or disclosure, covering both technical and physical measures. The exam point is using a case to show what breaching APP 11 looks like (a lost device, no access control) and what remedy is due.

The 2017 amendment establishes the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme (NDB) under the Privacy Act 1988. When personal information is subject to unauthorised access, disclosure or loss and this is likely to result in serious harm to the individuals concerned, it is a notifiable data breach: the organisation must assess it promptly, notify the affected individuals and the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner, and set out the measures already taken. Common mistake: treating every breach as notifiable and ignoring the likely to result in serious harm test.

Social engineering and phishing: impersonating a trusted organisation by email, fake websites, phone or SMS to steal account credentials. DoS overwhelms a service with traffic, and DDoS launches it from many sources through a botnet, which is harder to block. A back door bypasses normal authentication (hard-coded passwords, insecure remote tools) to leave long-term entry. IP spoofing forges the source address to pose as a trusted source. Common mistakes are confusing DoS with DDoS, or treating phishing as a purely technical flaw.

SQL injection stuffs malicious SQL into an input field so the database executes it and leaks or alters data; a man-in-the-middle attack intercepts or modifies packets between two parties, often helped by insecure Wi-Fi and IP spoofing; XSS injects malicious script into a trusted website so that it runs in someone else's browser, leading to session hijacking and information theft. The corresponding defences are parameterised queries and input validation, HTTPS and strong authentication, and output escaping with a content security policy. Common mistake: saying that XSS attacks the server.

A virus attaches itself to files and spreads only when its host is executed; a worm is a standalone program that copies itself and spreads automatically across networks; a trojan disguises itself as normal software to trick users into installing it; spyware secretly records user activity and sends the information back; adware forces ads on the user and malicious versions also track behaviour; ransomware encrypts data and demands a ransom. The exam point is telling virus from worm by how they spread. Common mistake: writing only that they are all malicious programs without the difference.

Physical threats are direct harm to hardware and the environment: devices stolen or lost, storage media carried away, cables and ports open to anyone, server rooms broken into. A zero-day vulnerability is a flaw the vendor has not yet found or patched, exploited by attackers before a fix exists, so the harm is great and defence is hard. Countermeasures include door access control and surveillance, encrypted storage, least privilege, prompt patching, layered defences and intrusion detection. Common mistake: assuming that installing antivirus software means you are safe.

The threat comes from people inside the organisation or from internal credentials: laptops and mobile devices lost or stolen leak data; passwords phished, weak or shared cause credential leakage; employees use their access to go beyond their authority, send data out or install unauthorised software. Defence rests on least privilege, multi-factor authentication, activity logs and auditing, offboarding and device return procedures, and regular training. Common mistakes are focusing only on external attacks, or equating every insider threat with a malicious employee.

Log analysis regularly reviews system and network logs to spot intrusion from unusual patterns such as masses of failed logins; anti-malware uses signature databases to detect and remove known viruses and ransomware; a firewall monitors and filters incoming and outgoing traffic by rules; ACLs use rules based on IP address, protocol or port to decide whether to allow or deny. An answer must match each measure to the threat. Common mistakes are thinking anti-malware is enough, or not knowing how ACLs and firewalls divide the work.

An IPS monitors traffic in real time and actively blocks suspicious behaviour (an IDS only alerts and does not block); a VPN builds an encrypted tunnel over an untrusted network to protect remote traffic; user training uses courses and simulated phishing to sharpen recognition of phishing, weak passwords and careless link clicking; an ICT code of conduct sets out acceptable use of IT resources, user responsibilities and the consequences of breaches; physical security protects equipment with access control, surveillance and locked racks. Common mistakes are confusing IDS with IPS, or listing measures without explaining the principle.

The standard framework for analysing a security incident: confidentiality means data is accessed only by authorised parties (disclosure breaks it); integrity means data is accurate and unaltered (modification breaks it); availability means authorised users can use the system when they need it (downtime from a DDoS breaks it). The method is to take an incident, first judge which one or more of the three it breaks, then give targeted protection. Common mistakes are conflating confidentiality with integrity, or answering only one of them and stopping there.

Three stages in controlling network access: authentication confirms who the user is (passwords, biometrics, multi-factor authentication); authorisation decides what that identity may do (permissions assigned by role, least privilege); and accounting records and traces their behaviour (logs, usage statistics), for later accountability and for finding anomalies. An answer should follow the chain of identity, permissions and activity record. Common mistakes are swapping authentication and authorisation, or omitting accounting altogether.

Symmetric encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt: it is fast and suits bulk data, but delivering the key safely to the other party is the hard problem; asymmetric encryption uses a key pair, with the public key openly shareable and used to encrypt or verify, and the private key kept by its owner and used to decrypt or sign, which solves distribution but is slow. A digital certificate is issued by a trusted certificate authority and binds a public key to the holder's identity, which is how a browser verifies that a website is genuine. Common mistake: reversing the uses of the public and private keys.

The early methods each had a fatal weakness: a substitution cipher replaces characters by a fixed rule and falls to letter frequency analysis; the Vigenere cipher combines plaintext and ciphertext using a repeating key, and once the key length is guessed frequency analysis still breaks it; mechanical encryption such as Enigma never encrypted a letter as itself; DES was the first digital encryption standard, but its 56-bit key is too short and falls to brute force on modern computing power. Common mistake: saying only that it is insecure without naming the weakness.

AES is the symmetric standard that replaced DES, with key lengths of 128, 192 or 256 bits, and it has not been broken; RSA is an asymmetric algorithm with 2048-4096 bit keys based on the product of large primes, secure but slow; ECC is a less resource-hungry asymmetric alternative with shorter keys and faster operations. Key management requires keeping private keys secret, backing them up off site, using keys long enough to resist brute force, and monitoring access with audit logs, following NIST guidance. Common mistake: mixing up the key lengths of AES and RSA.

Secure communication uses a hybrid scheme: first obtain the public key from the server's certificate and use asymmetric encryption to verify identity and safely agree a session key, then switch to symmetric encryption for the data itself. This is because asymmetric encryption is secure but slow, so it is used only to establish the connection, while symmetric encryption is fast and suited to carrying large amounts of data. In HTTPS the browser and server work exactly this way. Common mistakes are thinking the whole session is asymmetric, or not being able to say why two kinds are needed.

An ethical hacker simulates attacks under authorisation to find and fix vulnerabilities before a real attacker does, and the scope of testing can cover networks, applications, devices and even people (social engineering). The red team plays the attacker trying to break in, while the blue team is the internal defence, monitoring, detecting and responding to incidents and hardening the defences. All testing needs written authorisation and a defined scope, and any vulnerability found may only be used for fixing it. Common mistakes are reversing the red and blue roles, or ignoring authorisation and legal boundaries.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/CSC 计算机科学/Topic 4 ·: An entity is a real-world object to be recorded in the database (a student, a course), attributes are the characteristics describing an entity (student ID, name), and relationships describe the business links between entities, divided into one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many. For one-to-many, put a foreign key in the many table pointing at the primary key of the one side; many-to-many must introduce a linking entity and split into two one-to-many relationships; one-to-one can often be merged into a single table. Common mistakes are drawing a many-to-many as two tables joined directly, or putting the foreign key in the wrong table.

A table is how an entity is realised in the database. Fields (columns) define a kind of data and its type, records (rows) are individual instances, and the primary key uniquely identifies each row. In an answer, list the field names and data types first, then the constraints, and finally represent records in words or sample data. Common mistakes are swapping field and record, or forgetting the primary key so records cannot be uniquely identified and duplicates appear.

Five types you must know: integer stores whole numbers for numbering and counting; float stores decimals for measurement and averages; Boolean holds only true and false for states and flags; text stores strings for names, addresses and similar; date stores dates for birthdays and enrolment dates. The choice affects storage efficiency and which operations are possible. Common mistakes are storing postcodes or phone numbers as integers and losing leading zeros, or using float for money and getting precision errors.

A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table, and its values must be neither duplicated nor null; a foreign key is a field that references another table's primary key, used to create links between tables and enforce referential integrity; a composite key is a primary key made up of two or more fields together, unique only as a combination, and is common in linking tables that resolve many-to-many relationships. Common mistakes are treating a foreign key as necessarily unique (it may repeat), or setting a primary key on a field that can be null.

A non-normalised table produces three kinds of problem when data is added, changed or removed. Update anomaly: the same data is stored repeatedly across records, and changing only some of them makes it inconsistent. Delete anomaly: deleting one record also throws away other information that appeared only there. Insert anomaly: a record cannot be added because the data is incomplete. All three come from redundancy and poor dependencies, and the cure is normalisation. Common mistake: reciting the names without being able to give a concrete triggering scenario.

ODBC (Open Database Connectivity) is a standard interface that lets programs such as Python connect to a database and run SQL without rewriting code for each product, which is how a database interacts with other systems. A transaction is a group of operations that either all take effect or all roll back, and ACID means atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability, guaranteeing reliable data under concurrency and failure. A transfer is the classic example: the debit and the credit must belong to one transaction. Common mistake: attributing the four properties to the wrong terms.

A document recording the metadata of every element in the table structure, with five required columns: element name, data type, length or size, a brief description (what it stores, its format and default value) and constraints (unique or not, nullable or not, primary or foreign key). It is the basis for communication between developers and for later maintenance, so it must be written precisely rather than vaguely. Common mistakes are listing field names without constraints or descriptions, or setting the length too small for the real data that comes later.

Crow's foot notation shows entities and their relationships: entities as boxes with attributes listed inside, relationships as connecting lines, the crow's foot symbol on the many end, a small circle for optional participation and a bar for mandatory participation. The skill required is to read an ER diagram of up to 10 tables and to draw your own design of 3 to 8 tables. Common mistakes are putting a foreign key in the wrong table, missing the linking entity for a many-to-many relationship, and pointing the crow's foot and bar the wrong way.

Write the design as relation name(attribute1, attribute2, ...), with the primary key underlined and foreign keys marked FK. A many-to-many relationship must be split into three tables: one for each original entity plus a linking entity table whose primary key is a composite of the two primary keys, so that the same combination is never recorded twice. Common mistakes are writing only two tables yet claiming the many-to-many is resolved, or leaving one of the two foreign keys out of the linking table.

Three kinds of integrity keep data trustworthy. Referential integrity: a foreign key value must exist in the referenced table's primary key, otherwise orphan records appear. Domain integrity: a field's value must fall within the permitted type, range or format, enforced by data types, CHECK and NOT NULL. Entity integrity: the primary key is unique and not null, so every record can be uniquely identified. Common mistakes are swapping referential and entity integrity, or thinking a foreign key can point at any field.

Five angles for judging whether data is usable: currency, whether it is updated in time and still within its valid period; authenticity, whether the source is reliable and the data unaltered; relevance, whether it relates to the purpose of this analysis; accuracy, whether the values and formats are correct; and outlier removal, identifying and dealing with values that clearly deviate. An answer should judge each one and give a reason. Common mistake: deleting every outlier outright without first judging whether it is a data entry error or a genuine extreme case.

The first step of normalisation. 1NF requires every field to be an atomic value, with one item in a cell (not MATH1001, COMP1001), no repeating attribute groups (no columns such as Course1, Course2, Course3) and every record uniquely identified by the primary key. The method is to split the repeating attributes into a new table and add a foreign key in the original table pointing to it. Common mistake: splitting the comma-separated values but keeping the repeating columns.

The decisions turn on dependencies. 2NF: satisfy 1NF and have no partial dependency, meaning a non-key attribute must not depend on only part of a composite key (for example CourseName determined by Course alone); a relation whose primary key is a single field satisfies 2NF automatically. 3NF: satisfy 2NF and have no transitive dependency, meaning a non-key attribute must not depend on the primary key indirectly through another non-key attribute (for example ResultDescription determined by Result).

CREATE TABLE name(field type constraint, ...) creates a table, with PRIMARY KEY for the primary key, NOT NULL for required fields and UNIQUE for unique ones; MODIFY (ALTER TABLE in MySQL) changes a field's type or adds and removes constraints; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS removes a table. Constraints are the first line of defence for data validity. Common mistakes are dropping and recreating a table to change its structure, losing the data, or letting a foreign key's type drift out of line with the primary key it references.

Four basic statements: SELECT fields FROM table WHERE condition to query; INSERT INTO table(fields) VALUES(values) to insert; UPDATE table SET field=value WHERE condition to modify; DELETE FROM table WHERE condition to delete. Cascading deletes means that deleting a record in the parent table automatically deletes the records in the child table that refer to it, which maintains referential integrity. Common mistake: leaving out WHERE and changing or wiping the entire table in one go.

Five aggregate functions reduce many rows to a single value: COUNT counts rows, SUM totals them, AVG averages, MAX takes the largest and MIN the smallest. They are written as SELECT AVG(field) FROM table WHERE condition, usually with GROUP BY for per-group figures; combined with a calculated field they need an alias using AS, as in SELECT AVG(Grade) AS AverageGrade. Common mistakes are putting an aggregate function straight into WHERE, or taking SUM of a text field.

GROUP BY groups rows by a field before aggregate functions summarise each group; HAVING filters groups after grouping, whereas WHERE filters rows before grouping, which is the key distinction; ORDER BY sorts, ascending by default and descending with DESC; DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result. Common mistakes are putting an aggregate condition in WHERE, or omitting GROUP BY while summarising non-aggregated fields.

An inner join keeps only the rows where the join condition matches in both tables, written SELECT ... FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table1.foreign_key = table2.primary_key, and up to 4 tables can be joined; a calculated field derives a new value from an expression (such as unit price * quantity) and a concatenated field combines several text fields into one, both needing an alias with AS. Common mistakes are leaving out the ON condition, which produces a Cartesian product, or omitting aliases so field names are ambiguous.

AND requires both sides to be true, OR needs only one side true, NOT negates; BETWEEN tests whether a value falls within a range; IN tests whether a value belongs to a list; EXISTS tests whether a subquery returns rows; ANY is true when any one comparison holds; LIKE does pattern matching, where % stands for any number of characters and _ for a single character. Common mistakes are swapping what % and _ do, or writing the bounds of BETWEEN the wrong way round.

Ethical points to weigh when handling data: collecting personal information requires informed consent and only the necessary scope; respect individuals' control over their own data and anonymise where needed; verify that sources are reliable and accurate; credit the source when using other people's data; and make data mining transparent, avoiding algorithmic discrimination and the inference of sensitive information. An answer should use a case to show who is affected and what harm may follow. Common mistake: repeating that privacy must be protected without applying it to a situation.

Security and legal issues to handle when developing a database: store sensitive data encrypted; back up on a 3-2-1 strategy (3 copies, 2 on different local devices, 1 off site) and rehearse recovery regularly; restrict access on least privilege; and make data ownership and control explicit in contracts. Legally this corresponds to the Australian Privacy Principles: APP 5 notification of collection, APP 8 cross-border disclosure, APP 10 data quality, APP 11 security and APP 12 access rights.
AUSMAT May 2026 学习资料/CSC 计算机科学/语言、工具与考核资: Python is the programming language specified for the course and used in the ATAR exam, and in the real exam you must be able to write a working program directly; algorithm questions may be answered in SCSA standard pseudocode, whose conventions are given in the Additional Syllabus Support Booklet: keywords in capitals, structures explicitly closed, a single equals for assignment and a double equals for comparison. Revision focuses on being able to write and debug: control structures, functions and parameter passing, arrays and dictionaries, and the searching and sorting algorithms, all implemented independently.

The course uses SQLite for hands-on database work, since it needs no server and its syntax matches the syllabus; a guide to installing and using MySQL with VSCode is also available as an option; in design you draw ER diagrams in crow's foot notation and then write the design as relation name(attributes...) in relational notation. Common mistakes are skipping modelling and creating tables directly, which causes repeated rework, or not knowing the syntax well enough to write cross-table queries and grouped summaries.

For the networking part you must draw topology diagrams to the Cisco icon convention, using different icons for routers, switches, wireless access points and firewalls, and lines for links and subnets; the troubleshooting tools are ping, which checks whether a target is reachable and gives the round-trip time and packet loss, and traceroute, which shows the path hop by hop with the time for each. Common mistakes are mixing icons or leaving out end devices, or not knowing the troubleshooting order of pinging the gateway before running traceroute.

Neither the course nor the exam requires a graphical user interface: programs can use command-line input and output, and for databases you only need to run SQL at the command line or in a tool, so all your time should go into control structures, data structures, algorithms and table design. Knowing this stops you wasting effort on GUI libraries. Common mistake: spending a great deal of project time on an interface and squeezing out functionality and testing.

School-based assessment has four task types: the project examines the full technology process and its documentation, theory tests examine concepts and scenario analysis, practical tests require working code or SQL written within a time limit, and the examination covers everything. Prepare separately for each format: concepts by restating and explaining, practical work by writing code by hand repeatedly, and the project by keeping good design and test records as you go.

The external exam runs 3 hours with an extra 10 minutes of reading time; Section 1 is short answer and counts for 40%, Section 2 is extended response and counts for 60%. A Source Booklet of stimulus material is provided, and questions may ask you to analyse it; the material can include ER diagrams, network diagrams, data dictionaries, desk checking tables and pseudocode extracts. Manage your time, develop extended answers from the material, and avoid the common mistakes of ignoring the reading time and missing conditions in the material.

The lecture slides for the four topics, with the page counts directly reflecting how much each topic weighs: programming is heaviest (235 pages), data management next (163 pages), cyber security 72 pages and network communication 55 pages. Use this to allocate revision time; the slides explain every syllabus point with worked examples, so they suit consolidating along the main line after reading the textbook, checked against each topic's homework and past papers.

A collection of past WACE papers from 2016 to 2025 with each year's Source Booklet, the practice material closest to the real exam. Use it by sitting whole papers under time, then correcting every question against the marking approach afterwards, and summarising the question types that keep recurring, such as subnetting, normalisation to 3NF, multi-table SQL queries, Big O comparisons and error-type classification. Common mistake: reading the answers without writing, so in the exam you cannot produce the full working.

Reading material supplied with the course. The main part is Introduction to Scientific Programming with Python, which supplements Python syntax and programming approach; there is also cyber security reading covering attack types and technical detail. It suits going deeper than the slides, for example understanding how exception handling is written, common dictionary and list operations, and the technical mechanisms of attacks such as DoS and MITM.

Nine mentor worksheets arranged in increasing difficulty: the early ones practise arithmetic operations, selection and loops, pseudocode and desk checking tables; the middle ones move into network components and subnetting; the later ones cover database modelling, normalisation and cyber security. They suit immediate checking after each chapter, and questions you get wrong should send you back to the matching slides. Common mistake: doing only the questions you can already answer and skipping hands-on line-by-line exercises such as desk checks.

A collection of practical exercises and homework in varied formats: good programming practices presented as a group talk (explaining the practice, why it matters and comparing good and bad code), an infographic on network components, plus pseudocode rewriting, splitting functions and WACE past-paper practice. Answers to these tasks are in the Handouts in your personal section, so they can be used for self-testing. Common mistake: submitting without doing the work and missing the chance to code and draw by hand.

Course introduction material containing the full SCSA syllabus and the Additional Syllabus Support Booklet. The latter is the most practical quick-reference: pseudocode conventions and command tables, control structure examples, search and sort algorithm code, DoS and encryption methods, the protocol table for each layer, Cisco network icons, ER diagram and data dictionary examples, a full 1NF to 3NF derivation, and a table of common SQL syntax.

Four sections in OneNote that belong to you: Class Notes for key points from class, Handouts with the slides and the answers to all the homework, Homework holding each set of homework, and Quizzes with the tests so far. The most valuable for revision are the quizzes and the homework answers, which pinpoint the topics you keep getting wrong. Common mistake: only reading notes instead of redoing wrong questions, so the same errors come back in the exam.
